subject: technology
essential_question: How can understanding pictures, sounds, and simple data help us explain, decide, create, or solve something that matters?
standards: Michigan Computer Science: Data and Analysis
Michigan Computer Science: Impacts of Computing
project_brief: Collect a small set of data and create a simple picture graph with a short conclusion. This is the grade 3 culminating project for "Pictures, Sounds, and Simple Data" (ma-g3-tech-cs-u05, unit 5), built around sorting and counting objects, simple picture graphs, choosing a picture that fits, comparing two data sets, and who made this: source basics. Collect or use a small, fictional or already-approved data set related to sorting and counting objects, simple picture graphs, choosing a picture that fits, and comparing two data sets, and turn it into a labeled visual with a one-paragraph, evidence-based conclusion.
requirements: Address every topic listed for this unit: sorting and counting objects, simple picture graphs, choosing a picture that fits, comparing two data sets, who made this: source basics, and checking if a fact seems true.
Meet the performance task as written: Collect a small set of data and create a simple picture graph with a short conclusion.
Show your work or process, not just a final result — a process note, sketch log, commit history, or draft trail.
Complete the checklist in this package before submitting.
primary_task: Collect or use a small, fictional or already-approved data set related to sorting and counting objects, simple picture graphs, choosing a picture that fits, and comparing two data sets, and turn it into a labeled visual with a one-paragraph, evidence-based conclusion.
test_or_check_criteria: Every claim or design choice in the submission can be traced to sorting and counting objects or another named topic from this unit — nothing is left unexplained.
The submission runs, displays, or demonstrates correctly on at least two different sample inputs or scenarios the student chooses.
No real password, API key, account credential, precise location, or other real personal/system data appears anywhere in the submission — fictional or sandbox examples only.
The student can explain, in their own words, why each step or decision was made, not just that it works.

presentation_and_privacy.sandbox_and_credentials_note: This project never touches a real account, a real password or API key, a live production system, or another person's real data. Use fictional names, sandbox environments, local files, or already-approved sample data throughout. Submit code, screenshots of your own sandbox, diagrams, or a written walkthrough — a live public deployment is never required.

copyright_and_authorship: The final submitted work must remain your own authorship. A parent, tutor, or AI assistant may help you plan, explain a concept, demonstrate a technique, or give feedback on a draft, but may not produce the graded work itself. Never request, store, or submit a real password, API key, access token, or other real credential; use only fictional accounts and sandboxed or offline systems.
remediation: If the project stalls, step back to the smallest version of the task: rebuild just the part covering sorting and counting objects in isolation, using a worked example from this unit as a model, then re-attach it to the full project once that smaller piece works and you can explain why.
extension: Once the core project is working, extend it to handle a new constraint or edge case related to simple picture graphs, or compare two different approaches to the same problem and explain the real tradeoff between them in your own words.
